newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's largest city elects first black mayor.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's largest city elects first black mayor.

text.p: Sao Paulo, Brazil's largest city and economic powerhouse, elected its first black mayor by an overwhelming margin on Friday in runoff municipal balloting.
Early results showed Celso Pitta, a U.S.-educated accountant and political neophyte, enjoyed a 28 percentage point lead over his only opponent, former mayor Luiza Erundina.

Pitta's victory shattered a long held view that Sao Paulo voters would never elect a black person to the mayor's office, although more than half the city's 6.7 million voters are either black or of mixed race.
His election should also prove a boost for his political mentor, incumbent mayor Paulo Maluf, who is preparing a run for the presidency in the 1998 national elections.
The Sao Paulo race was the most closely watched of 31 mayoral elections across the country involving over 20 million voters.
After lengthy campaigns that focused on local issues of transport, health care and crime, the elections promised few surprises.
Electoral officials said voting went smoothly although over 100 people were arrested in Campo Grande, the capital of Matto Grosso state, after an attempt to pack ballot boxes.
Troops were also called out in three state capitals -- Maceio, Manaus and Natal -- for fear of clashes between supporters of rival candidates.
In Rio de Janeiro, Brazil's second largest city, Luiz Paulo Conde of the right wing Liberal Front Party (PFL) beat Sergio Cabral of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Social Democrat Party (PSDB).
